headline: High: Copilot can read repo/editor context while Argo Workflows can move artifacts over networked workflows, creating default-path data leakage and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no browser or clipboard bridge, and B has no MCP or shell execution, so direct injection paths are limited. However, B reads editor buffers and repo context, while A operates on artifacts/parameters via REST/GRPC workflows; if A’s outputs are pasted or surfaced into B’s context, prompt-like content could influence Copilot. The pairwise bridge is indirect, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF A outputs are manually copied into B editor buffers or repo context, then instruction-like content can influence B.
IF B is used on files derived from A artifacts, then prompt injection becomes possible through file content.
mitigations: Keep A outputs out of editor buffers unless reviewed.
Strip instructions from artifact text before opening in Copilot.
Use a separate review file for A-generated content.
Mark untrusted workflow outputs as data, not prompts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches artifacts and parameters and can egress over allowlisted network paths; B reads repo context and open buffers and sends context to api.githubcopilot.com. That creates a default-path leakage route if sensitive artifacts or parameters from A are placed into B-visible files. The pair is not fully isolated, so medium fits the documented overlap.
conditions: IF A artifacts or parameters contain secrets or regulated data and are opened in B-visible files, then B can transmit that context to GitHub Copilot.
IF the same repository/workspace is used for both agents, then file-level leakage is possible.
mitigations: Keep sensitive A outputs outside the repo workspace.
Use redacted copies for Copilot review.
Separate workflow artifacts from code buffers.
Disable Copilot on files containing sensitive pipeline outputs.
Review allowlisted egress destinations for A before sharing outputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can operate on workflow artifacts and B can write the filesystem and modify git state. B also supports multiple instances with per-editor sessions, but there is no explicit locking across the pair. If both touch the same repo or artifact directory, concurrent edits and git-state conflicts are plausible in default use, though not as severe as unrestricted shared writes.
conditions: IF A and B target the same working tree or artifact directory, then concurrent writes can conflict.
IF B modifies git state while A updates workflow-generated files, then merge or overwrite conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate directories for A and B outputs.
Serialize edits with a simple handoff checklist.
Commit or snapshot before running B on A outputs.
Avoid concurrent runs against the same repo.
Use read-only copies for review when possible.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s Workspace/chat flow can treat repo context and open buffers as authoritative inputs, while A can generate artifacts and parameters that may be consumed downstream. If A’s outputs are fed into B without verification, B may propagate incorrect workflow-derived facts into code or documentation. The interaction is plausible in default workflows, but human review reduces blast radius.
conditions: IF A-generated artifacts are used as source material for B, then unverified errors can cascade into B outputs.
IF B edits code or docs based on A outputs without cross-checking, then downstream mistakes can propagate.
mitigations: Require a verification step before B uses A outputs.
Annotate A outputs with provenance and timestamps.
Cross-check critical facts against original sources.
Limit B to drafting, not finalizing, A-derived content.
Keep a human approval gate for any A-to-B handoff.

E_compliance.rationale: A is docs-only and touches artifacts/parameters with allowlisted egress, while B is a closed-source GitHub Copilot service that sends editor context to GitHub. The profiles do not show PHI, EU-only data, or a residency mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is evident: different retention/processing expectations for shared code or artifacts. The other agent is cited because the mismatch arises from their combined handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into shared repo buffers, then Copilot processing may create a policy mismatch.
IF A artifacts contain data subject to stricter retention than GitHub Copilot’s handling, then compliance review is required.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Copilot-visible files.
Use a separate compliant workspace for sensitive artifacts.
Review vendor retention terms before sharing outputs.
Redact identifiers before opening files in Copilot.
Document which data classes may flow between the tools.
